markedBy: Antigravity manual semantic assessment before live model evaluation; not an independent human rater
description: Held-out evaluation dataset of 12 questions with newly added key points across 6 domains (evaluation, agents, inference, RAG, Debug this, coding), with 3 hand-authored answers each (strong, partial, weak).

genai-eval-llm-as-judge.title: How do you design an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation harness and mitigate systematic biases?
genai-eval-llm-as-judge.answer: An LLM-as-a-judge evaluation harness should use an explicit scoring rubric with few-shot reference examples for each score tier rather than open-ended 1-to-5 ratings. To combat position bias, swap the ordering of paired candidate completions and take the average or flag inconsistencies. Verbosity bias requires explicit instructions penalizing length without substance and pairing with length-normalized metrics. Self-enhancement bias is mitigated by evaluating models from different families (e.g., using Claude 3.5 Sonnet to judge GPT-4o outputs). Finally, calibrate the automated judge against a gold standard set of expert human ratings to compute Spearman rank correlation or Cohen's kappa, tracking inter-annotator agreement to establish confidence thresholds.
keyPoints: Use an explicit scoring rubric with examples.
Swap answer order to counter position bias.
Control verbosity bias and use a different model family.
Calibrate against human labels and track agreement.

genai-eval-rag-triad-hallucination.title: How do you evaluate RAG systems for hallucination using the RAG Triad?
genai-eval-rag-triad-hallucination.answer: The RAG Triad framework evaluates retrieval-augmented generation across three distinct stages to localize failures: 1. Context Relevance: Evaluates whether the retrieved chunks are relevant to the user's input query, flagging noise from retrieval. 2. Faithfulness (Groundedness): Assesses whether the model's response is strictly supported by the retrieved context alone, identifying hallucinations or unverified external assertions. 3. Answer Relevance: Evaluates whether the final response directly addresses the user's inquiry, catching evasive or off-target completions. Scoring each edge of the triad independently enables precise diagnosis—revealing whether quality issues stem from chunking/retrieval or generator drift.
keyPoints: Faithfulness checks claims against retrieved context.
Context relevance evaluates the retrieved passages.
Answer relevance checks whether the response addresses the question.
Score each link separately to localize failures.

genai-agent-react-tool-calling.title: How does an autonomous ReAct agent loop work and how do you prevent runaway execution?
genai-agent-react-tool-calling.answer: A ReAct (Reason + Act) loop coordinates an LLM through alternating steps: Thought (reasoning about the current state and plan), Action (selecting a specific tool and arguments), and Observation (incorporating the environment's response into working memory). Runaway execution is mitigated through: 1. Strict step limits (e.g., capping total turns at 10-15). 2. Wall-clock execution and token-expenditure budgets. 3. Schema validation via JSON Schema or Pydantic before tool invocation. 4. Cycle detection heuristics that monitor consecutive identical tool calls or semantic repetition and trigger graceful fallback or human intervention.
keyPoints: ReAct cycles through thought, action and observation.
Validate tool calls against clear schemas.
Enforce step, time and cost budgets.
Detect repeated calls and stop or hand off gracefully.

genai-agent-single-vs-multi.title: When should you build a multi-agent system versus a single agent with multiple tools?
genai-agent-single-vs-multi.answer: Start with a single agent using structured tools; single agents are easier to debug, have lower latency, and cost less. Graduate to a multi-agent architecture when: 1. Tool context exceeds the model's reliable decision boundary (e.g., >15-20 distinct tools confusing selection). 2. Sub-tasks require fundamentally incompatible system prompts, roles, or security sandboxes. 3. Long tasks generate token volume that crowds out reasoning context. Use a supervisor or hierarchical pattern where a coordinator delegates to specialized sub-agents with narrow toolsets, ensuring each agent operates on focused context. Always measure quality improvement against the compound latency, token cost, and inter-agent coordination failure modes.
keyPoints: Start with a single agent.
Split agents when tool choice or unrelated context becomes a problem.
Use a supervisor with focused contexts and tool sets.
Measure quality gains against extra latency, cost and failure modes.

genai-cost-latency-ttft-tpot.title: How do you measure and optimize Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and Time-Per-Output-Token (TPOT)?
genai-cost-latency-ttft-tpot.answer: Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and Time-Per-Output-Token (TPOT) must be measured separately across percentiles (p50, p90, p99) because they correspond to distinct computational bottlenecks. TTFT represents prompt prefill latency plus queuing delay, dominated by compute-bound matrix multiplications over the input tokens. Optimize TTFT through prompt pruning, prompt caching (e.g., shared prefix reuse), speculative prefill, and separate prefill/decode worker pools. TPOT measures the autoregressive decode phase, which is memory-bandwidth bound due to loading full model weights for each generated token. Optimize TPOT using continuous batching, weight quantization (FP8, INT4), tensor parallelism, speculative decoding, and smaller model architectures.
keyPoints: Measure TTFT and output-token time separately using percentiles.
TTFT reflects queueing and prompt prefill.
Shorten prompts and cache shared prefixes for TTFT.
Improve decode with batching, quantization or a smaller model.

genai-serving-kv-cache-pagedattention.title: Why does the KV cache bottleneck LLM serving memory, and how does PagedAttention solve it?
genai-serving-kv-cache-pagedattention.answer: The Key-Value (KV) cache stores past token key and value projections across all attention heads and layers during autoregressive generation to avoid quadratic recomputation. Memory requirements scale linearly with context length, batch size, number of layers, and hidden dimension—often consuming 60-80% of GPU VRAM at high concurrency. Traditional serving frameworks allocated contiguous physical memory based on the theoretical maximum sequence length (e.g., 4K or 8K tokens), causing 60-80% memory waste through internal fragmentation and reserved headroom. PagedAttention (introduced by vLLM) solves this by partitioning the KV cache into fixed-size physical blocks (e.g., 16 tokens), mapping virtual sequence tokens to non-contiguous physical blocks via a block table, and enabling copy-on-write sharing of common prefixes across requests.
keyPoints: KV cache stores prior tokens' keys and values in every layer.
Cache memory grows with tokens and concurrent requests.
Maximum-length contiguous allocations waste memory and fragment it.
PagedAttention allocates blocks on demand and can share prefixes.

genai-chunking-strategies.title: How do you choose chunk size and chunking strategy in a production RAG system?
genai-chunking-strategies.answer: Chunk size selection balances semantic specificity against contextual completeness. Small chunks (128-256 tokens) yield precise vector embeddings that match specific facts cleanly, but risk losing broader paragraph context and inter-sentence dependencies. Large chunks (512-1024 tokens) preserve comprehensive context but dilute embedding vectors with peripheral topics and consume scarce prompt context. The optimal chunking strategy mirrors document structure: use hierarchical or markdown-aware chunking that splits on semantic headers and tables rather than fixed character offsets. Incorporate a 10-20% sliding token overlap to prevent splitting entities across boundaries. Always benchmark chunk sizes empirically against gold-standard retrieval evaluation datasets using hit rate and MRR.
keyPoints: Choose chunking from document structure and user questions.
Small chunks improve precision but lose context.
Large chunks dilute embeddings and consume more tokens.
Use overlap and tune on labelled retrieval evaluations.

genai-dense-vs-sparse-search.title: Why do production retrieval systems combine dense vector search with sparse keyword search?
genai-dense-vs-sparse-search.answer: Dense vector search (bi-encoders) excels at semantic understanding, synonym matching, and cross-lingual retrieval, but struggles with exact keyword hits, rare domain terminology, acronyms, product codes, and out-of-vocabulary entities. Sparse search (BM25, SPLADE) excels at exact lexical matching and inverted-index keyword precision, but fails on semantic paraphrasing and conceptual relevance. Combining both in hybrid search provides defense-in-depth: sparse catches precise identifiers while dense surfaces conceptual relevance. Because dense similarity scores and sparse BM25 scores inhabit different numerical distributions, use Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) or a cross-encoder reranker to normalize and blend ranked outputs rather than adding uncalibrated raw scores.
keyPoints: Dense retrieval finds semantic paraphrases.
Sparse retrieval preserves exact names, codes and rare terms.
Hybrid search covers their different failures.
Fuse by rank when raw score scales differ.

senior:debug-retrieval-recall-drop-reind.title: After re-indexing 2M documents with a new HNSW index in Milvus, top-10 retrieval recall dropped from 89% to 64% while query latency dropped from 42ms to 8ms. How do you triage this?
senior:debug-retrieval-recall-drop-reind.answer: A simultaneous drop in recall (89% -> 64%) and latency (42ms -> 8ms) is a textbook signature of reduced search scope in approximate nearest neighbor search. In HNSW, `ef_search` (the size of the dynamic candidate list during query traversal) controls the recall-latency tradeoff. An engineer likely re-indexed with a drastically reduced `ef_search` (e.g., from 128 to 16) or default search parameters, causing the search to terminate early in the graph. Check `ef_search`, graph connectivity parameter `M`, vector normalization, and distance metric consistency. Sweep `ef_search` on a held-out test query set to trace the recall/latency Pareto curve, restore `ef_search` to the optimal operating point, and gate future index deployments behind an automated 500-query recall evaluation suite.
keyPoints: Check ef_search, M, vector normalization and distance metric.
Sweep ef_search against held-out queries.
Restore ef_search from 16 to 128.
Gate index promotion on 500 gold queries.

senior:debug-continuous-batching-ttft-ta.title: After enabling continuous batching in vLLM with max_num_seqs=256, p50 time-to-first-token stayed flat at 110ms, but p99 TTFT jumped from 180ms to 2,850ms during peak 40 req/s load. What is happening?
senior:debug-continuous-batching-ttft-ta.answer: In continuous batching with shared worker pools, prompt prefill and token generation share the same GPU execution iterations. When peak load brings long-context prompts, compute-heavy prefill operations preempt or delay the scheduling of new prompt prefills behind ongoing decode steps, causing head-of-line blocking in the scheduler queue. Additionally, with `max_num_seqs=256`, KV cache memory pressure triggers KV swap-outs to CPU or request preemptions. To diagnose, correlate p99 TTFT with prompt length distributions and monitor preemption metrics. Fix by: 1. Enabling chunked prefill (`--enable-chunked-prefill` with max batched tokens capped at 2048) to interleave prefill chunks with decode steps. 2. Tuning `max_num_batched_tokens`. 3. Architectural disaggregation: separating prefill-specialized instances from decode instances (PD disaggregation).
keyPoints: Correlate TTFT with prompt length and track preemptions.
Long prefills block queued generations.
Enable chunked prefill and cap batched tokens at 2048.
Separate prefill and decode worker pools.

senior:coding-chunker-token-aware.title: Implement a token-aware recursive text chunker in Python with configurable overlap and sentence boundary preservation. What would you test?
senior:coding-chunker-token-aware.answer: A production token-aware chunker must measure lengths using the actual model tokenizer (e.g. tiktoken or HuggingFace tokenizers) rather than character counts. The recursive algorithm splits along a hierarchy of delimiters: double newlines (paragraphs), single newlines, sentence-ending punctuation (., ?, !), and finally whitespace words. It accumulates splits until adding the next would exceed `max_tokens`. When emitting a chunk, it retains the trailing `overlap_tokens` to seed the next chunk, preserving narrative continuity. Test suites must cover: 1. Single sentences that exceed `max_tokens` (must force-split without infinite loops). 2. Tiny inputs shorter than `max_tokens`. 3. Zero-token or whitespace-only inputs. 4. Multibyte Unicode characters and emojis. 5. Overlap continuity: ensuring the suffix of chunk N exactly matches the prefix of chunk N+1 in token space.
keyPoints: Count tokenizer subwords rather than raw characters.
Split by paragraphs, then sentences, then words as needed.
Emit at the token limit and retain trailing overlap.
Test oversized sentences, small documents, Unicode and overlap continuity.

senior:coding-bm25-from-scratch.title: Implement Okapi BM25 scoring from scratch in Python given inverted document frequencies, term frequencies, and document lengths. What edge cases must you handle?
senior:coding-bm25-from-scratch.answer: Okapi BM25 scores a query against a document using the formula: score = sum(IDF(q_i) * (TF(q_i, D) * (k1 + 1)) / (TF(q_i, D) + k1 * (1 - b + b * (|D| / avgdl)))). The term frequency saturation is controlled by parameter k1 (typically 1.2-2.0), preventing high frequency terms from dominating, while parameter b (typically 0.75) penalizes document length relative to average corpus length. Edge cases to handle: 1. Empty documents (|D| = 0), preventing zero-division in length normalization. 2. Terms with zero document frequency (unseen query vocabulary). 3. Highly frequent terms appearing in >50% of corpus resulting in negative IDF (apply standard floor IDF >= 0 or Robertson-Spärck-Jones smoothing). 4. Query terms not present in the document. 5. Purely lexical limitation: BM25 cannot capture semantic synonyms, requiring query expansion or dense blending in production.
keyPoints: Combine inverse document frequency with saturated term frequency.
Normalize by document length so length alone does not dominate.
Handle empty documents, unmatched queries and unseen vocabulary.
BM25 favors exact lexical matches but misses semantic synonyms.

examples.answer: When building an automated model judge, provide a detailed criteria checklist with few-shot demonstration exemplars for every score tier. To defeat position bias where models prefer whichever answer comes first, run pairwise evaluations twice with swapped candidate order and discard or tie conflicting outputs. Guard against length bias by prompting the judge to penalize verbosity and evaluate with a different LLM family than the generation model. Finally, validate the judge against a curated dataset of expert human annotations and monitor Cohen's kappa or rank correlation over time.

We create structured grading rubrics containing concrete grading criteria and sample inputs. We also compare the automated judge decisions with human reviewer grades to measure percentage agreement before deploying it into CI.
Just ask GPT-4 if the answer looks good on a scale of 1 to 10 without any guidance. The model naturally knows what quality looks like, so no rubrics, examples, or human checks are required.

The RAG triad isolates the failure points across the pipeline. Faithfulness verifies that every factual proposition asserted in the response is strictly grounded in the retrieved chunks without hallucinations. Context relevance verifies that the retrieved documents actually pertain to the user prompt rather than returning noisy distractors. Answer relevance checks whether the synthesized completion directly answers the original inquiry. By evaluating these three stages independently, you immediately pinpoint whether errors originate in retrieval or synthesis.

Faithfulness tests whether the generated response is completely supported by the provided source documents. Answer relevance ensures the model actually addressed the user's specific prompt instead of wandering off-topic.
Measure user engagement by tracking how long people stay on the search page. If users spend more than three minutes reading, the retrieval system is considered highly accurate.

The ReAct pattern alternates between reasoning steps, invoking tools, and observing the environment feedback in an iterative loop. To avoid unbounded loops, parse and validate arguments strictly against JSON Schema or Pydantic models before executing. Hard limits must be placed on total iteration steps, wall-clock execution time, and cumulative token or dollar cost. In addition, the runtime should detect duplicate consecutive tool calls with identical arguments, breaking the cycle and falling back to a graceful error or human-in-the-loop escalation.
ReAct works by alternating thought reasoning, calling external functions, and reading the resulting observations. Every tool call must be strictly validated against typed schemas before execution.
Let the agent run infinitely without step caps because modern frontier models never get stuck in loops. Schema validation is unnecessary because the LLM generates valid Python directly.

Always begin with a single agent having a clean toolset. You should only transition to a multi-agent architecture when confusing tool selections or bloated context windows degrade decision accuracy. When decomposing, employ an orchestrator or supervisor pattern where specialized sub-agents operate within isolated contexts and narrow tool boundaries. Crucially, quantify whether accuracy improvements outweigh the compounded round-trip latency, monetary token spend, and new inter-agent communication failure modes.
Always default to starting with a simple single-agent pattern. Decompose into multiple agents only when the number of conflicting tools overwhelms the model's prompt context.
Immediately design a swarm of ten autonomous agents for every simple task. Having more agents always reduces latency and guarantees lower cloud costs without any coordination complexity.

Track TTFT and per-token decode latency independently, reporting p50, p90, and p99 distributions. TTFT is dominated by scheduler queue time and the initial compute-bound prompt prefill phase. To optimize TTFT, trim bloated prompt templates and utilize KV cache prefix sharing or prompt caching for common system instructions. To accelerate per-token generation, utilize continuous batching, apply INT8 or FP8 weight quantization to reduce memory bandwidth pressure, or distill to a smaller parameter count.
TTFT reflects the queue wait time and initial prompt prefill computation. You can accelerate TTFT by pruning long system instructions and using KV prefix caching.

TTFT measures the time to generate each token during the autoregressive output phase, whereas TPOT is the queueing delay before the first token arrives. You optimize TTFT by quantizing weights and optimize TPOT by increasing temperature.

In transformer generation, the KV cache retains computed key and value activations across every layer for all generated tokens to avoid recomputation. Cache consumption scales linearly with context length and the number of active concurrent user sessions. Traditional runtimes pre-allocate contiguous memory based on the worst-case maximum sequence length, leading to severe internal and external memory fragmentation. PagedAttention borrows virtual memory paging principles from operating systems, allocating non-contiguous physical blocks on demand and enabling copy-on-write sharing of identical system prompt prefixes across streams.
The KV cache preserves key and value vectors from earlier tokens across all attention layers. Total memory footprint expands with sequence length and concurrent requests.
The KV cache stores the model's static weight matrices in L1 CPU cache so they do not need to be loaded into GPU VRAM. It never grows during inference.

Chunking strategy must align with document layout (such as markdown headers or tables) and expected user query granularity. Small text segments maximize embedding precision for targeted factual lookups but risk severing contextual prerequisites. In contrast, massive chunks dilute dense vector representations and consume excessive prompt token capacity. Maintain a rolling overlap between chunks to preserve sentence continuity and systematically tune chunk parameters against a labeled retrieval evaluation benchmark using hit-rate metrics.
Tiny chunks increase retrieval precision but lose broader contextual meaning. Oversized chunks dilute semantic signals in vector representations and take up too much context window space.
Always split documents into exactly 50-character slices regardless of sentence boundaries. Never use overlap because overlap corrupts vector databases.

Dense embeddings excel at conceptual semantic search, finding paraphrased concepts even when terminology differs entirely. Conversely, sparse keyword retrievers like BM25 excel at exact keyword matches, part numbers, SKUs, and rare entity names that dense models compress away. Combining both in a hybrid pipeline mitigates their respective blind spots. Because cosine similarity and BM25 scores operate on incomparable scales, merge their retrieved candidate lists using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) based on rank positions rather than uncalibrated raw scores.
Dense vector search captures semantic meaning and conceptual paraphrasing. Sparse BM25 retrieval protects exact keyword matches, serial numbers, and uncommon domain jargon.

Dense retrieval is for looking up exact product codes and rare acronyms without fuzzy matching, whereas sparse retrieval calculates high-dimensional dense vector embeddings to discover conceptual synonyms. You should only use sparse search for semantic understanding.

First inspect the HNSW index hyperparameters, specifically ef_search, M, vector L2 normalization, and the configured distance metric (IP versus L2). The dramatic drop in both latency and recall strongly indicates ef_search was drastically lowered during the reindex. Run a sweep of ef_search values against a held-out test query set to trace the recall versus latency Pareto frontier. Increasing ef_search from the misconfigured 16 back to 128 will restore the missing recall while keeping latency reasonable. Finally, implement an automated CI gate requiring index updates to pass recall thresholds on 500 golden validation queries before production promotion.
Examine HNSW parameters like ef_search, M, distance metrics, and vector normalization. Sweep ef_search across a holdout query set to find the sweet spot between latency and recall.
The recall drop means Milvus ran out of disk space. Reinstall Ubuntu on the database server and switch to MySQL full-text search.

Begin by analyzing latency logs to correlate TTFT spikes with incoming prompt token lengths and check engine metrics for sequence preemptions. In unified serving, long prefill requests monopolize GPU compute and starve queued decode steps. To resolve this, activate chunked prefill with a max batched token limit of 2048 to interleave prefill and decode execution. For sustained high traffic, disaggregate the architecture into dedicated prefill and decode worker pools, passing KV activations over high-speed interconnect.

Correlate the TTFT measurements against input prompt length and inspect whether KV cache eviction preemptions are occurring. Long compute-heavy prompt prefills are monopolizing the GPU and blocking waiting requests.
The issue is that continuous batching was designed for image generation models, not text. Disable batching entirely and serve one user at a time per server.

When building a token-aware recursive chunker, compute chunk size using the actual model tokenizer's subword token count rather than raw character lengths. Implement recursive splitting that hierarchically breaks text by double newlines, then sentence boundaries, and finally whitespace when chunks exceed limits. Build chunks up to the configured token ceiling, retaining trailing tokens to form the specified overlap with the next chunk. Validate with unit tests covering sentences larger than the max chunk size, single-word documents, multi-byte Unicode/emojis, and verify that the overlap retains exact token sequences.

Token counting must use the tokenizer's subword encoder instead of character counts. Split recursively starting with paragraph breaks, then punctuation sentences, and falling back to individual words.
Split the text string with regex on commas and write to a CSV file. Tokenizers are irrelevant for chunking because text is just ASCII characters.

Okapi BM25 scores documents by multiplying inverse document frequency (IDF) with a non-linear, saturating term frequency (TF) function parameterized by k1. It penalizes verbosity by normalizing term frequency by document length relative to average corpus length scaled by parameter b. In implementation, handle boundary conditions including empty documents, zero matching query terms, negative IDFs for ubiquitous terms, and out-of-vocabulary words. Remember that BM25 rewards exact lexical token overlap but cannot capture semantic synonyms or conceptual paraphrasing.

BM25 combines an IDF calculation with term frequency that saturates as counts increase. It normalizes by document length divided by average document length so long texts do not score high purely on size.
BM25 is a deep neural network with 12 transformer layers that generates dense 768-dimensional embeddings. It does not use document length or term frequencies.
